name: After Hours Agenda
summary: A custom streetwear store built around the clothes. Product pages, size guidance, a shopping bag, and checkout.
challenge: After Hours Agenda is Little Fight’s own independent clothing brand. Its store needed to keep that identity visible.
Customers need garment details, sizing, and clear steps to checkout. The lookbook should help them explore the clothes.
approach: Built connected paths through collections, product pages, and the shopping bag.
Placed size guidance, shipping details, returns, and contact options nearby.
delivered: Live online store with collections, product pages, and size selection.
Shopping bag, checkout, lookbook, and customer-support pages.
outcome: Live at afterhoursagenda.com. Visitors can browse garments and choose sizes before checkout.
imageAlt: After Hours Agenda storefront with priced garments and shopping links, October 23, 2026.
narrative: The store keeps the black-sheep mark and rose accent. Clothing leads the page, with prices and shopping links visible.
Product pages bring garment views, size choices, and measurements together. The lookbook and support pages sit alongside the shopping path.

name: Army & Navy Bags
summary: A phone-first design concept for a neighborhood shop, with product groups, hours, and directions close at hand.
challenge: The old website acted mostly like a listing and did not explain why a new neighbor or traveler should visit.
The concept needed to retain the shop’s real Lower East Side character without turning it into a generic retail template.
approach: Built a phone-first path from store character to product groups, hours, call, and directions.
Used a neighborhood map to situate the shop near familiar nearby stops.
delivered: A design concept with shop imagery, product groups, local facts, and one-tap directions.
Desktop, tablet, and phone layouts.
outcome: A design concept for an easier shop visit, from first look to directions.
imageAlt: Army & Navy Bags concept artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: The concept treats the store as part of a Lower East Side walk. It begins by showing the place and what it carries, then keeps practical visit details close.
It shows an approach to a phone-first neighborhood guide.

name: Brothers Pizzeria
summary: A neighborhood-pizzeria design concept that brings heritage, a readable menu, and phone ordering together.
challenge: The initial digital menu buried the family story and compressed the price grid on smaller screens.
The design needed to bring the shop’s history forward while preserving all menu details and prices.
approach: Reframed the page as a printed neighborhood handbill with the family story before ordering.
Designed menu lines to stack cleanly on phones and kept the call action close.
delivered: A design concept with a complete menu, phone-first ordering, and a matching brand kit.
Desktop, tablet, and phone layouts.
outcome: A design concept for a menu and ordering path that stays clear on a phone.
imageAlt: Brothers Pizzeria concept artwork published by Little Fight NYC.
narrative: The concept centers the family history and keeps it connected to practical menu and ordering tasks. It is built as a readable neighborhood handbill rather than a generic restaurant page.
It shows an approach to a restaurant website where the menu and first call are easy to find.

name: CC Films
summary: Fans get the trailer in one tap, press gets reviews and coverage, and anyone can ask about a screening, all on the film’s official home.
challenge: Marrow needed one official home without losing the film’s mood.
Fans, press and festival guests each arrive wanting something different.
approach: The official trailer at the top of the page, one tap away.
Reviews, press coverage and film databases gathered in one section.
A contact form sorted by press, distribution, collaboration and viewing questions, plus a 224-photo premiere archive.
delivered: Film website and responsive layouts.
Premiere photo archive with photographer credit.
Press, review and screening-inquiry paths.
outcome: Live at ccfilms.net, with separate paths for viewers, press and screening questions.
imageAlt: CC Films website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: CC Films needed atmosphere and clear facts at the same time. The trailer, reviews, credits and archive each have their own place.
Film credits and premiere photography stay with their original creators. We built the website, gallery and connected paths.
metaDescription: CC Films case study: the official website for Marrow, with the trailer up front, press and reviews in one place and a path to ask about screenings.

phone.alt: CC Films live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

name: Chromatic Painting & Design
summary: Homeowners see the finished work first, then ask for a painting estimate in one form, with a separate path for mural commissions.
challenge: Painting and mural work share the craft but start with different questions.
An estimate request had to collect enough to quote without feeling like paperwork.
approach: Project photos lead, ahead of any service list.
One estimate form with seven required answers: name, city, how to reply, project type, what needs paint, timing and details. A photo is optional.
A separate commission path for murals, under the same studio name.
delivered: Website and project portfolio.
A painting estimate form and a mural commission path.
Contact paths by call, text or email.
outcome: Live at chromaticaz.com, with separate estimate and mural commission paths.
imageAlt: Chromatic Painting & Design website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The design puts finished work ahead of a generic service list, so a visitor sees the quality before they are asked for anything.
Painting and mural pages keep one studio identity while giving each customer the right question for their job.
metaDescription: Chromatic Painting & Design case study: a Phoenix painter and muralist portfolio with a short estimate form and a separate mural commission path.

desktop.alt: Chromatic Painting & Design live website on desktop, captured October 27, 2026.

phone.alt: Chromatic Painting & Design live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

action.detail: The live estimate form: location, surface, timing and an optional photo.

name: ClearHelp
summary: A production resource-finding site that starts with people’s situations and locations, with a separate route for offering help.
challenge: People seeking food, housing, or other resources may have little time, energy, or privacy.
Finding help and offering help needed distinct starting points.
approach: Organized public paths around needs, ZIP search, plain-language navigation, and resource information.
Kept quick-exit guidance visible and separated public use from private staff work.
delivered: Public website and need-based paths.
ZIP search, resource information, and nearby guidance.
Separate public paths for people seeking and offering help.
outcome: Live at clearhelp.org with separate first steps for finding help and offering it.
imageAlt: ClearHelp website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: ClearHelp begins with a situation or place, instead of assuming someone knows an agency name. Familiar language and category paths lead into the resource directory.
Separate routes support people looking for resources and people offering help, with location-based information and clear next steps.

name: Easy Tiger Bar
summary: Tonight’s menu, upcoming events and a photo journal of the bar, readable on a phone, with one QR menu address that stays current.
challenge: Guests want the current menu, what’s on this week and directions, usually from a phone at the door.
The bar needed to update menus and event posters without guests seeing a half-finished draft.
approach: The menu as real text, on the homepage and at one QR address that never changes.
Upcoming events with dates and times, linked to the bar’s Eventbrite page.
A photo journal of 39 photos, sorted by people, drinks and the room.
delivered: Guest website, text menu, events and gallery.
A QR menu page and a draft-to-publish editing flow.
outcome: Live at easytigerglendale.com, with one maintained menu address for the website and the QR code.
imageAlt: Easy Tiger Bar website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The guest side shows the room, the drinks and what’s on, then hands over directions and hours.
On the owner side, menu and poster changes are saved as drafts first, so a change can be prepared before guests see it.
metaDescription: Easy Tiger case study: a Glendale neighborhood bar site with a text menu, upcoming events, a photo journal and one QR menu address.

desktop.alt: Easy Tiger Bar live website on desktop, captured October 27, 2026.

phone.alt: Easy Tiger Bar live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

action.detail: The live menu page, the same address the table QR code opens.

name: Grand Funding LLC
summary: Investors land on the loan they need, by deal type and city, and every page says terms come only after a real review.
challenge: An investor searching for a bridge or fix-and-flip loan in a specific city needs a page that answers that search, not a general homepage.
Grand Funding focuses on business-purpose real estate financing and sets terms deal by deal, so no page could imply a standard offer.
approach: A page for each loan type: fix-and-flip, bridge, construction, cash-out refinance, second position and land.
City pages for Phoenix, Scottsdale, Los Angeles and San Diego, plus side-by-side comparisons and a glossary of lending terms.
The same boundary everywhere: business-purpose focus, terms set after a transaction review, and no commitment to lend.
delivered: Loan-type, city, comparison and glossary pages.
A quote request that asks for the deal basics.
Lending disclosures for Arizona and California.
outcome: Live at grandfundingllc.com. Every loan page leads to a quote request or a call.
imageAlt: Grand Funding LLC website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: Each page answers one search an investor actually makes, then asks for the deal basics: loan type, property location and target close.
Terms are never published. Grand Funding reviews the deal and provides them in writing.
metaDescription: Grand Funding case study: business-purpose loan pages by deal type and city for Arizona and California investors, built to be found and honest about terms.

desktop.alt: Grand Funding LLC live website on desktop, captured October 27, 2026.

phone.alt: Grand Funding LLC live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

action.label: Request a quote
action.detail: The live quote path: send the deal basics for a transaction review.

proof.schema: Organization, WebPage and BreadcrumbList details, so each loan page is read as part of one lender

name: Hair By Rachel
summary: Every item on Rachel’s menu has its own Book button, each main service has a page, and AI assistants get a plain guide to the studio.
challenge: A new color client needs to know what to book first, what it may cost, and that Rachel approves each request before it is confirmed.
Search engines and AI assistants can only recommend what they can read: the services, the studio, and how to book.
approach: A page for each main service: balayage, color correction, blonde, extensions and curly hair, each leading to booking.
A booking page that explains the Square handoff, the card hold and Rachel’s approval before the calendar opens.
Business details written for machines too: structured data in every page and a plain-text guide for AI assistants at /llms.txt.
delivered: Website design, service pages, consultation and first-visit guides, and Spanish pages.
A Square booking path with the policy explained up front.
Structured data and an llms.txt guide for AI assistants.
outcome: Live at hairbyrachelcharles.com. Every service on the menu leads to a booking path.
imageAlt: Hair By Rachel website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The site makes room for two kinds of visitor: someone ready to book, and someone who only knows their hair goal. The consultation and first-visit pages give the second visitor a place to start.
Square stays the booking system. Each service, its starting price and the first-visit context come before the calendar.
metaDescription: Hair By Rachel Charles case study: a Phoenix stylist site with a page for each main service, a clear Square booking path and details AI assistants can read.

desktop.alt: Hair By Rachel live website on desktop, captured October 27, 2026.

phone.alt: Hair By Rachel live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

action.label: Book with Rachel
action.detail: The live booking page: choose a service, then continue to Square.

proof.schema: HairSalon, an OfferCatalog of services and a ReserveAction for booking

extra.label: Lower running cost
extra.text: We reworked how the site reads its booking data. Database compute fell 89%, from 23.3 to 2.5 GB-hours a day. That is our own hosting measurement, not a client sales figure.

name: Legacy Music Group
summary: A Dallas recording studio’s original website, restored with its look and motion intact.
challenge: Restore the studio’s website. Keep the look, movement, and pages its visitors know.
approach: Kept the original design and made the paths to studio services, engineers, and booking work across screen sizes.
delivered: 35 restored pages with the original design, motion, and booking links.
outcome: Visitors can explore the studio website, then open Legacy’s existing booking page to choose a session.
imageAlt: Legacy Music Group restored website on desktop.
narrative: The dark design and moving gallery set the mood. Clear pages explain the studio, its team, and the work you can book.
Visitors can read about a service, meet the engineers, and open the studio’s booking page.

name: Logan Loans
summary: A mortgage-information site that gives buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors distinct routes to learn before contacting the lender.
challenge: Different audiences arrive with different questions, which a single generic sales page cannot explain well.
approach: Built responsive layouts and routes for buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors.
Connected public guides, planning tools, and contact paths while keeping planning separate from loan offers.
delivered: Website design, audience paths, public guides, planning tools, and contact options.
outcome: Live at logan.loans. Planning figures help people prepare questions; loan terms remain with the lender.
imageAlt: Logan Loans website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The site sorts a broad mortgage topic by visitor situation. Readers can browse guides and planning tools before choosing a contact path.
A calculator result is not a loan offer; the lender confirms terms after reviewing the person, property, and loan.

name: The Break Room
summary: People searching for pool or darts in Glendale land on a page about exactly that, and groups send their night plan in one form.
challenge: Someone nearby searches for a pool hall or darts in Glendale and needs the tables, the boards and the way in, fast, on a phone.
Groups needed a simple way to share a plan, without a form that pretends to reserve the room.
approach: Pages that match what people search: a pool hall in Glendale, darts in Glendale, food and drinks, and what’s on.
A group request form: occasion, date, guest count and what the night should include, then a call to confirm.
Real room photos labeled as real, kept separate from the campaign artwork.
delivered: Venue website with pool, darts, menu and events pages.
A group and private-event request form.
Map, call and directions paths on every page.
outcome: Live at thebreakroompoolhall.com, with a group request path and a call button within reach.
imageAlt: The Break Room website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The opening says what the room has: 13 pool tables, 8 dart boards, food and sports. Menu, events and directions are one tap away.
The group form says plainly that a request is not a reservation. The room confirms by phone.
metaDescription: The Break Room case study: Glendale pool hall and darts pages built for “near me” searches, a readable menu and a group request form.

name: The Tarot Hotline
summary: Booking comes first: pick a reading, share your question, and see current prices from Square before you pay.
challenge: Visitors may know their question but not which reading fits it.
Prices and openings change, so the site could not show a number that might be stale.
approach: Three readings with clear formats: a voice-note reading within 24 hours, a 30-minute session and a 60-minute session.
A five-step booking flow: your reading, your question, about you, time and format, then review.
Current prices load from Square, and payment happens on Square’s secure page.
delivered: Website, reading pages and first-reading guidance.
A five-step booking flow connected to Square.
outcome: Live at thetarothotline.com, with booking as the main path on every page.
imageAlt: The Tarot Hotline production homepage on desktop.
narrative: The Tarot Hotline makes the reading format and the next step clear before anyone pays.
First-reading guidance sits beside the booking flow for people who have never had a reading.
metaDescription: The Tarot Hotline case study: a booking-first site where visitors choose a reading, share their question and see current Square prices before paying.

desktop.alt: The Tarot Hotline live website on desktop, captured October 27, 2026.

phone.alt: The Tarot Hotline live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

action.label: Start a reading
action.detail: The live booking flow: choose a reading, then review before Square checkout.

proof.schema: Service and Offer details with a ReserveAction for booking

name: VenueCircuit
summary: A live venue-operations demo with a shared show record, role-specific workspaces, and nightly close-out tools.
challenge: A venue night spans events, people, inventory, and money. The product needed one shared demo record that makes each role legible.
approach: Built public demo paths around command and show search, recent workspaces, role-specific controls, and the nightly close-out.
Kept production demo data explicitly fictional.
delivered: Public platform with 56 product paths, 14 demo seats, and nine investor chapters.
Scoped command and show search, recent workspaces, role artwork, responsive controls, and motion.
outcome: Live at venuecircuit.app with a public demo. The demo uses sourced listings and fictional operations.
imageAlt: VenueCircuit public owner-demo workspace on desktop.
narrative: A public owner-demo workspace shows a shared show record alongside search, workspaces, controls, and the nightly close-out.
The demo uses sourced listings and fictional operations. It does not represent a deployed venue account.

name: Stephenie Powers
summary: Every service on Stephenie’s menu has its own Book button into Square, with a guide page for each kind of appointment.
challenge: A new client choosing between a cut, color, highlights or extensions needs to see the options and book the right one.
A long salon menu is hard to use on a phone, and the wrong booking costs everyone time.
approach: Guide pages for haircuts, men’s cuts, color, blonde and highlights, color correction and extensions.
A booking page where every service has its own Book button into Square.
First-visit, pricing and FAQ pages for the questions people ask before they book.
delivered: Website design and service guide pages.
A booking page with a Square link for each service.
First-visit, pricing, FAQ and portfolio pages.
outcome: Live at stepheniepowershair.com. Every service on the menu leads to its own booking button.
imageAlt: Stephenie Powers website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The opening shows Stephenie’s style and puts Book with Stephenie on the first screen.
The service menu is grouped the way clients think about it, so the right appointment is one tap from its guide.
metaDescription: Stephenie Powers case study: an Uptown Phoenix stylist site where every service on the menu leads straight to its own Square booking button.

name: Hiraya Group
summary: Contractors and restoration teams find the estimating help they need and start a file, with a separate plain-language page for property owners.
challenge: Roofers, restoration crews and builders each arrive with a different job: a new repair estimate, a missed item, or a bid to write.
Property owners with an insurance claim needed their own starting point, not a page written for contractors.
approach: A page for each service: Xactimate estimating, supplement support, construction bids and estimating partnerships.
Guides and a document checklist that help a team gather the right files before the first conversation.
A separate page for property owners that explains the service and asks where the property is first.
delivered: Website design and service pages.
Resource guides and a document checklist.
A contact path for estimate and claim questions.
outcome: Live at hirayagroup.net, with a separate starting point for contractors and for property owners.
imageAlt: Hiraya Group website capture published in the Little Fight NYC case study.
narrative: The opening speaks to the person with photos on their phone and a deadline, then sorts them by the work in front of them.
Fees and the first step are explained before a visitor is asked to get in touch.
metaDescription: Hiraya Group case study: an insurance estimating site with a page for each service, file-prep guides and a separate page for property owners.

desktop.alt: Hiraya Group live website on desktop, captured October 27, 2026.

phone.alt: Hiraya Group live website on a phone, captured October 27, 2026.

action.detail: The live contact page for estimate questions.

name: DeckSpace
summary: A product design concept that brings an onboard guide, guest network, and memory layer into one cruise experience.
challenge: Guests need events, venue hours, and each other without digging through a dashboard.
approach: Keep the nostalgic heart of cruising and organize discovery around the voyage.
delivered: A product design concept covering onboard discovery, profiles, events, and shared photos.
outcome: A design concept for helping guests find the moments and people around a voyage.
